entries.title: As freed ComEd defendants face new trial, jurors say they already considered ‘every aspect’ of the case
entries.summary: <p>Before they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" target="_blank" >freed two former ComEd officials</a> who went to prison over an alleged corruption scheme<b> </b>involving Illinois’ most powerful politician, federal appeals court judges asked a lot of questions about the case — but mostly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/11/3/23919713/corruption-jurors-ed-burke-trial" target="_blank" >about the jury</a> that found the pair guilty.</p><p>For example, how could the judges be sure the jury didn’t focus solely on bribery claims that have since been undermined by the U.S. Supreme Court?</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times asked three of the 12 jurors Wednesday. They said they carefully considered every claim leveled against former ComEd CEO Anne<b> </b>Pramaggiore and longtime ComEd lobbyist Michael McClain — including those that survived a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2024/06/26/supreme-court-snyder-ruling-madigan-corruption" target="_blank" >2024 Supreme Court ruling</a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" >Ex-ComEd CEO, Madigan ally to be freed from prison as appeals court calls for new trial in conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“We concluded they all intertwined and related to each other,” Robert<b> </b>Garnes, one of the jurors in the 2023 ComEd conspiracy trial, told the Sun-Times.</p><p>The ComEd trial <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/2/23697452/jurors-reach-verdict-in-comed-bribery-trial" target="_blank" >ended with the convictions</a> of McClain, Pramaggiore<b> </b>and two others of a plot to bribe<b> </b>ex-Illinois House Speaker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news" target="_blank" >Michael J. Madigan</a>. The high court’s later decision to limit a key bribery law undermined the verdict and led to the dismissal of the bribery counts in 2025. But convictions for conspiracy and falsifying books and records remained.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Then the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals took things further Tuesday. It promised to order a new trial and told the feds to release Pramaggiore and McClain from their two-year prison sentences “forthwith.”<b> </b>The news came four hours after a three-judge panel heard arguments in the case.</p><p>The Federal Bureau of Prisons confirmed the release of McClain and Pramaggiore late Wednesday afternoon.</p><p>The appeals court’s order had no direct impact on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/mike-madigan-guilty-verdict" target="_blank" >Madigan’s separate conviction</a>, which came in February 2025. The 2023 trial of McClain and Pramaggiore also ended with the convictions of longtime ComEd lobbyist John Hooker and former City Club President Jay Doherty, but they did not appeal and have served their sentences.</p><p>During Tuesday’s arguments in the ComEd case, Judges<b> </b>Thomas<b> </b>Kirsch<b> </b>and<b> </b>Joshua<b> </b>Kolar<b> </b>seemed particularly concerned with the remaining conspiracy conviction against McClain and Pramaggiore.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/11/3/23919713/corruption-jurors-ed-burke-trial" >‘Facts and common sense’: Chicago’s corruption jurors reflect on past trials as Ed Burke’s case nears</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It featured multiple “objects”<b> </b>for the jury to consider, including bribery and falsifying records.</p><p>Given the feds’ emphasis on bribery during the trial, as well as the Supreme Court’s ruling, the judges wanted assurance that jurors reached a verdict that included false records as an object of the conspiracy, rather than an invalid bribery theory.</p><p>“Here’s the problem,” Kirsch told a prosecutor. “When you charge the case and try the case as a bribery case, what’s to say the jury just didn’t consider the illegal bribery object in the conspiracy and stop right there?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure “was actually one of the last ones we looked at,” even though it appeared as Count One<b> </b>in the indictment.</p><p>“That was the big behemoth of it all,” Goldenberg said. “We actually did really parse it out and look at each individual charge and looked at each object of it.”</p><p>Another juror, Amanda<b> </b>Schnitker Sayers, agreed with Goldenberg’s recollection. She said, “we almost worked it backwards” during the 27-hour deliberations.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" >Ex-ComEd CEO, Madigan ally to be freed from prison as appeals court calls for new trial in conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“For each individual count we took them all separate and we went through and we found the evidence for each one,” Schnitker Sayers said.</p><p>Garnes said it all “went hand in hand.”</p><p>“We took in every aspect of the trial that was presented before us,” he said.</p><p>The jurors’ comments are unlikely to influence what happens next in the case. But they provide insight that’s otherwise unavailable in the courtroom. Schnitker Sayers raised a concern about future efforts to invade the privacy of the jury room, though.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: Sky's Skylar Diggins wanted to be closer to home, but she’s not just coasting into retirement
entries.summary: <p>To be a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> fan right now is to be bursting with questions. Ones like: What is Skylar Diggins doing in Chicago?</p><p>It surprised many to see the seven-time All-Star choose a team that has won less than 30% of its games over the last two seasons, and an organization not exactly known for flawless execution since its 2021 championship.</p><p>So how did she end up here?</p><p>As the new collective-bargaining agreement reshaped the league this offseason, Diggins took a moment to reflect.</p><p>She thought about where she was in her career — 35 years old, two kids, entering her 12th season — and decided she wanted a change. She's played on the West Coast her whole career, but she grew up in South Bend, 90 miles outside of Chicago.</p><p>She wanted to be closer to home.</p><p>And Chicago successfully sold her on its vision: a win-now roster that was tougher, more athletic, more competitive than last year.</p><p>For head coach Tyler Marsh, Diggins' arrival is proof the organization is moving in the right direction.</p><p>"Skylar has been around this league a long time to know the fake from the real," Marsh said. "And there's a reason she wanted to be here. Being close to home helps, but you also gotta be able to trust the people you're going to compete with. There's some discernment there that she's able to recognize."</p><p>The Sky did execute well in free agency, landing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/04/14/azura-stevens-returns-to-chicago-where-the-fit-and-the-money-made-sense" >stretch big Azurá Stevens</a> and two-way wing DiJonai Carrington, and adding young talent in Rickea Jackson and Jacy Sheldon.</p><p>But executing the "win-now" part won't be easy. Most of the league's top teams retained their cores. And even with all the added talent, Diggins is still the Sky's only All-Star.</p><p>Which means the Sky better hope she didn't come back to the Midwest just to decompress before retiring.</p><p>Lucky for them, she shot down the idea before anyone thought to raise it.</p><p>"I'm not just coming here saying this is the end or whatever for me," she said at her introductory news conference. "I don't think it'll be a diminishing return. I'm committed to the work. … I want to get better. That's been my mantra since I was a kid — 'get better.' That's the mindset I have here for this organization, for myself, and that's the standard I hold myself to."</p><p>Even for players with the highest standards, some decline in their game is inevitable. Over the last two years, Diggins' scoring average has settled around 15, down from the 17-20 range of her prime. But pair that with six assists and you're still looking at one of the best point guards in the league.</p><p>So, Sky fans: is this great-player-comes-home-at-the-tail-end-of-her-career storyline giving anyone a Candace Parker flashback? Will this homecoming end in a championship, too?</p><p>One can hope. But there are a few big differences between then and now. As good as Diggins is, she's not quite Parker. And Parker came home to a roster that had been together for years. Diggins is walking into a complete overhaul.</p><p>She'll need a little magic to bring them together ahead of schedule.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: After quick struggles for Shane Smith, White Sox aim to 'slow down his world' at Triple-A
entries.summary: <p>After an awful opening week, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>’ starting rotation has been a bright spot with an MLB-best 1.73 ERA in 11 games from April 3-14.</p><p>If you were told in spring training that Sox starters would go on a heater like that, you probably would’ve expected Opening Day hurler <b>Shane Smith </b>to be on top of his game — not down on the farm trying to rediscover his All-Star form from last season.</p><p>For Smith to run it back to the big leagues, he’s got to stop running away from the pitch that made him a Rule 5 success story, general manager <b>Chris Getz</b> said a week after the surprising demotion.</p><p>“He was running away from using his four-seam fastball. Just the overall quality of that pitch, along with his curveball, just wasn't up to his standard,” Getz said of the righty, who covered only 8⅓ innings in his three Sox starts, surrendering 12 runs before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/04/08/white-sox-option-opening-day-starter-shane-smith-to-triple-a-charlotte" target="_blank" ><u>getting shipped to Triple-A Charlotte</u></a>. “We felt like it was best to kind of slow down his world a little bit, get him in an environment that is not so focused on getting so deep into games, or even win the ballgame."</p><p>Smith looked a little better in his last big-league game, but had another uneven outing in his first go with the Knights over the weekend, giving up three runs on four hits with a walk and five strikeouts in four innings.</p><p>“There’s always a cascade effect when you have starters not going deep into games. It starts affecting bullpens,” Getz said. “He definitely made progress in the most recent outing up here at the major league level, but we know that he can be so much better, and he acknowledges that as well.”</p><h3><b>Pre-game scare</b></h3><p>Attendees at Rate Field were left in a stunned silence before Wednesday’s game when <b>Gerald Chaney</b> collapsed while singing "Lift Every Voice and Sing” on Jackie Robinson Day.</p><p>Chaney, a longtime national anthem performer and beloved ballpark presence, was alert as paramedics treated him on the field. He was taken to a hospital for further evaluation and treatment, according to the Sox.</p><h3><b>Schultz in the rotation</b></h3><p>Manager <b>Will Venable</b> confirmed that rookie lefty <b>Noah Schultz</b> has a regular spot in the Sox’ starting rotation after his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/14/noah-schultz-white-sox-mlb-debut" target="_blank" ><u>shaky MLB debut</u></a> Tuesday night — no surprise, but an assertion that Getz stopped short of making a day earlier.</p><p>Schultz consistently flashed 98 on the radar gun and struck out four while laboring through 4⅓ innings, giving up four runs but rebounding from some first-inning jitters.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure in the big leagues."</p><p>Soft-spoken in the clubhouse but intense on the mound, the 6-10 Schultz credited big sisters <b>Emily Schultz</b> and <b>Ashley Schultz</b> with sharpening his on-field edge in their childhood Wiffle ball games in the backyard while <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/13/noah-schultz-white-sox-debut-aurora-oswego-east" target="_blank" ><u>growing up in Aurora</u></a>.</p><p>“They helped get that competitive spirit in me. It started at a young age,” Schultz said. “I can’t thank them enough. They have been with me through it all. It’s so awesome to have their support and have them in the stands.”</p><h3><b>Coming and going</b></h3><p>As part of the Sox’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/15/sam-antonacci-called-up-white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>latest roster shuffle</u></a> bringing up prospect <b>Sam Antonacci</b>, they also recalled veteran lefty reliever <b>Tyler Gilbert</b>, optioned <b>Brandon Eisert</b> to Charlotte and designated outfielder <b>Dustin Harris</b> for assignment.</p><p>Harris was a hero of Sunday’s win at Kansas City, robbing a potential home run in right field. He went 3-for-12 with a double, four walks and a pair of stolen bases in six games with the Sox.</p><p>Venable said they’ll send him to Charlotte if he clears waivers.</p><p>“It was a really tough decision. … He was really just kind of the odd guy out, really not because of anything he did,” Venable said.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true"
